title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text: Ongoing real-world studyENAR 2025 poster

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Overview
This ongoing retrospective clinical-outcomes study compares traditional polypectomy with vaginoscopy polypectomy during pregnancy, considering both procedural outcomes and time to preterm birth.

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Analytical problem
The study asked whether outcomes differed by surgical approach, whether effects varied between cervical and decidual polyps, and which demographic, clinical, or postoperative factors were associated with preterm birth.

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Why it matters
Traditional forceps-based polypectomy can involve bleeding and discomfort during pregnancy. Vaginoscopy polypectomy is a less-invasive alternative, but its safety and effectiveness relative to traditional surgery—across cervical and decidual polyps—require careful evaluation. The study therefore considers procedural burden and obstetric follow-up together.

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
My contribution
I serve as the lead statistician: I designed the statistical analysis plan, collaborate with clinicians at Jiangxi Maternal & Child Health Hospital who collect the confidential real-world data, and conduct the primary statistical analyses. I was also the presenting author of the ENAR 2025 poster.

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Data and study design
The study uses confidential real-world data from pregnant patients treated at Jiangxi Maternal & Child Health Hospital. The analysis includes baseline characteristics, surgical measures, postoperative complications, and obstetric follow-up. Participant-level data are not distributed through this site.

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Statistical methods

Descriptive comparisons using chi-square, t-test, or Wilcoxon procedures as appropriate
Kaplan–Meier curves for gestational age at delivery
Cox proportional hazards models for preterm birth risk
Adjusted modeling using clinically relevant covariates and backward variable selection

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Results and practical contribution
The ENAR poster reported no significant difference in the total count of adverse events between surgical groups. Vaginoscopy polypectomy was associated with shorter procedure time and lower bleeding in selected comparisons, while recurrent bleeding and high white-blood-cell count were associated with preterm-birth risk. These interim observational findings motivate continued analysis; they should not be interpreted as randomized comparative-effectiveness or formal noninferiority evidence.

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Limitations
The study was retrospective and relatively small. Potential confounding, subgroup instability, selection into treatment, and the censoring assumptions used for time-to-event analysis limit causal and clinical interpretation.

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Outputs

title: Cervical Polypectomy During Pregnancy
text:
Reproducibility and availability
Only the approved conference poster is public. The real-world participant-level data and analysis dataset remain confidential.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text: Exploratory master’s thesisAward-recognized · Not peer-reviewed

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Overview
This exploratory thesis investigated whether autopsy-derived neuropathological staging could inform time-dependent Alzheimer’s disease progression probabilities and clinical-trial planning. It compared a pseudo-longitudinal approach with longitudinal imaging data and identified important limitations involving early-stage prediction, measurement, sample size, and generalizability.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Research questions

What are time-dependent pathological progression probabilities after accounting for demographic characteristics and APOE genotype?
How might progression models inform theoretical sample-size calculations for trial populations with specified characteristics?

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Why it matters
Longitudinal neuropathological measurement is difficult, and trial populations often underrepresent important groups. Autopsy data provide detailed endpoint staging but require strong assumptions when used to reconstruct progression over time.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
My contribution
I developed and presented this exploratory MS thesis analysis under the supervision of Professor Rebecca Betensky, comparing pseudo-longitudinal and longitudinal approaches and translating the model outputs into theoretical trial-planning calculations.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Data and study design
The work used NACC autopsy data as a cross-sectional source and ADNI-3 as a longitudinal source. The NACC analysis modeled endpoint Braak stage and CERAD score using disease-duration and participant characteristics. The ADNI-3 analysis used repeatedly observed imaging-derived progression classifications for comparison.


01NACC autopsy dataCross-sectional endpoint staging


02Ordinal stage modelingBraak stage and CERAD score


03Pseudo-longitudinal probabilitiesTime-dependent exploratory derivation


04ADNI-3 comparisonLongitudinal imaging-derived progression


05Trial calculationsTheoretical sample-size scenarios

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Statistical methods

Cumulative ordinal logistic models for NACC neuropathological stages
Logistic regression for ADNI-3 progression classifications
Derivation of time-dependent progression probabilities under simplifying transition assumptions
Consideration of education, race/ethnicity, sex, age, APOE genotype, and cognitive status
Theoretical sample-size calculations with fixed power and effect-size inputs

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Results and practical contribution
The project demonstrated a workflow for comparing autopsy-derived pseudo-longitudinal estimates with a longitudinal source and for translating model scenarios into trial-planning calculations. It did not establish external validation, clinical readiness, or proven gains in trial efficiency.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Limitations

The look-backward approach may be biased for early progression because premortem information is limited and the manner of death is not modeled.
The simplifying assumption that individuals progress no more than one pathological stage per time unit may miss faster progression.
PET processing, threshold selection, and early-stage sensitivity can introduce measurement and classification error.
The ADNI-3 comparison had limited sample size and waves, particularly for later progression.
Racial, cognitive-status, education, and income imbalances in NACC and ADNI constrain representativeness and generalizability.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Outputs

 NYU Thesis Recognition Award Innovative Topic or Approach · Class of 2024

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Progression and Clinical-Trial Design
text:
Reproducibility and availability
This page presents the study design and acknowledged limitations without redistributing NACC or ADNI data. No validated prediction tool is offered.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text: Peer-reviewed collaborative studyPublished 2026

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Overview
This real-world natural-history study characterized survival, mortality risk, and clinical manifestations across the lifespan for Barth syndrome, an ultra-rare, life-limiting genetic disorder. It combined the Barth Syndrome Foundation’s larger intake dataset with its longitudinal patient/caregiver registry.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Research problem
Formal analyses of Barth syndrome survival and clinical progression have been limited by the rarity of the condition, small longitudinal samples, staggered registry entry, and incomplete information for some risk factors.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Why it matters
We analyzed the largest and most detailed available cohort of patients with suspected or confirmed Barth syndrome assembled to date, representing all deceased and living cases known to the Barth Syndrome Foundation at the time of analysis. This real-world evidence can help collaborators recognize periods of elevated risk, understand how manifestations change with age, and identify priorities for care and future research.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
My contribution
I collaborated with the Barth Syndrome Foundation and NYU Langone and co-led the statistical design and analysis exploring risk factors for survival and symptomology. I also contributed to translating statistical results for clinical and foundation collaborators and am first author of the publication.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Data and study design
Two related cohorts were analyzed:

An overall cross-sectional cohort of 502 individuals from the Foundation’s intake dataset, representing more than 80% of known global cases at the time of analysis.
A longitudinal registry cohort with up to 11 years of follow-up and more detailed patient/caregiver-reported clinical information.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Statistical methods

Descriptive characterization of demographic and clinical manifestations
Kaplan–Meier survival estimation for the overall and longitudinal cohorts
Risk-set adjustment for staggered entry in the registry cohort
Cox proportional hazards models for mortality-related outcomes
Multiple imputation by chained equations for selected incomplete risk factors
Sensitivity analyses separating confirmed and suspected cases

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Results and practical contribution
The study identified early childhood as a period of substantial mortality risk and described increasing clinical burden across the lifespan. By pairing broad case ascertainment with a more detailed longitudinal registry, the analysis provides a stronger empirical foundation for clinical discussion and future natural-history research while keeping cohort-specific uncertainty visible.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Limitations
The larger intake cohort is susceptible to survival and ascertainment bias because follow-up time was not consistently available. The longitudinal cohort was smaller, contained few survival events, and had limited repeat symptom surveys, producing wide uncertainty for some estimates. Self- or caregiver-reported clinical information and missing data also constrain interpretation.

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Outputs

title: Survival and Clinical Progression in Barth Syndrome
text:
Reproducibility and availability
The public repository provides the R analysis code. Participant-level registry data are not published through this portfolio.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text: Methodological researchOngoing

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Overview
I am developing extensions of regression-based multiple imputation for studies that contain both scalar measurements and functional observations such as neuroimaging or EEG trajectories. The work adds a functional-principal-components-regression approach for imputing missing scalar variables within the fregMICE framework, evaluates the method through large-scale simulation, and applies the workflow to multimodal clinical and EEG data.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Research problem
Complete-case analysis can discard substantial information when high-cost multimodal data are incomplete. Existing multiple-imputation practice is mature for scalar data, but mixed missingness across functional and scalar variables creates additional modeling and uncertainty challenges.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Why it matters
Biomedical studies increasingly collect densely measured functions alongside demographic, treatment, and clinical variables. An imputation strategy that uses both information types may reduce information loss while respecting uncertainty—provided its performance and limitations are evaluated carefully.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
My contribution
I developed the functional-principal-components-based extension, designed and implemented the simulation study, ran reproducible large-scale evaluations on GW’s Pegasus high-performance computing environment, and applied the workflow to multimodal clinical and EEG data. I presented the simulation work at GWSPH Research Day 2026 and contributed to the JSM 2026 paper.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Data and study design
The methodological evaluation includes samples of 100 and 350 under 10%, 20%, and 30% missingness, with scalar-only and mixed-missingness scenarios and both smoother and bumpier functional settings. The developing workflow is also being applied to multimodal clinical and EEG data from a major-depressive-disorder study.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Statistical methods

Functional regression multiple imputation by chained equations (fregMICE)
FPCR- and penalized-functional-regression approaches for missing scalar variables
Penalized function-on-function regression for missing functional responses
Rubin’s-rule pooling and comparison of alternative covariance estimators
Simulation evaluation using bias, error, coverage, interval width, and computation time

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Results and practical contribution
The approved poster reports that the functional-regression imputation approaches generally tracked the simulated targets more closely than complete-case analysis. Performance became more difficult at higher missingness and near complex functional features, and interval performance was sensitive to the covariance estimator. The real-data application extends the work beyond the poster’s simulation-only time point; application-specific results are not summarized here before final review.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Limitations
Simulation scenarios necessarily simplify the range of functional shapes, missing-data mechanisms, covariance structures, and downstream analyses seen in practice. The EEG application provides an important real-data check, but one application cannot establish performance across biomedical settings. Additional sensitivity analyses and external applications remain part of the ongoing work.

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Outputs

 GW Research Day poster Approved public PDF · Doctoral Research prize   JSM 2026 session and slides Innovative Methods in Mental Health Statistics · Contributed paper   GWSPH Research Day recognition Official departmental award record

title: Functional Regression-Based Multiple Imputation for Mixed Missing Data
text:
Reproducibility and availability
Approved poster and conference materials are linked above. Research code and application data are not distributed through this site.

title: About
text:
I am a PhD candidate in the Biomedical and Health Data Science program, Biostatistics track, at George Washington University. My route into the field began with management science at Ocean University of China, continued through an MS in Biostatistics at New York University, and now centers on methodological and collaborative biomedical research at GW.
I am most interested in statistical questions that arise when biomedical data are incomplete, functional, longitudinal, high-dimensional, or time-to-event. Across projects, I try to connect careful inference and validation with a clinically meaningful question—not add complexity for its own sake. I also aim to be a strong statistical storyteller: making theory, assumptions, and uncertainty understandable to collaborators and external audiences, and translating them into practical approaches for real-world problems.

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text: ENAR DataFest 2026 WinnerCompetition project

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
Overview
Our GWU team evaluated whether integrating high-dimensional molecular information could improve breast-cancer survival prediction beyond traditional clinical variables. The project won first place at ENAR DataFest 2026.

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
Analytical problem
Multi-omics data can add biological detail while also increasing dimensionality, instability, and the opportunity for overfitting. The central question was not simply whether a more complex model could fit the available data, but whether its predictive value held across validation settings.

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
Why it matters
Responsible biomarker modeling requires evidence that additional complexity improves prediction in a repeatable way. Comparing clinical-only, single-omics, and integrated approaches helps separate occasional gains from dependable improvements.

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
My contribution
I served as the GWU team leader, coordinating analytical decisions, model comparison, interpretation, and the final team presentation. I also created the analytical workflow used to organize and communicate the team’s end-to-end approach.

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
Data and study design
The competition used breast-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, accessed through cBioPortal. Inputs included clinical variables, mRNA expression, DNA methylation, and somatic mutation information. We compared clinical-only models with single-omics, multi-omics, and prior-knowledge-informed feature representations.

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
Statistical methods
The analysis used a nested validation framework to compare feature sets and model families while keeping final testing separate from model development. I created the analytical workflow below to organize and communicate the team’s end-to-end approach.

  

End-to-end analytical workflow created by Kexin Fu for the GWU ENAR DataFest 2026 project. Select the figure to view it at full resolution.




View an accessible workflow summary



Define cohortsOverall survival cohort and complete multi-omics subset


Create nested splitsHeld-out test set with repeated outer training and validation folds


Prepare omics featuresMissingness filtering, imputation, standardization, variance filtering, and correlation pruning


Select featuresData-driven Cox screening plus mutation- and GWAS-informed alternatives


Assemble comparisonsClinical-only, single-omics, combined multi-omics, and prior-informed feature sets


Fit and tune modelsElastic-net Cox, random survival forest, and DeepSurv


Evaluate predictionOuter-fold C-index and integrated Brier score, followed by held-out testing and risk stratification


Interpret signalsFeature importance and exploratory Bayesian survival analysis

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
Results and practical contribution
Clinical-only models generally performed as well as or better than models that added omics data. Among the omics configurations, mRNA tended to add more predictive value than methylation, while prior-informed feature construction did not consistently outperform data-driven selection. No model family dominated every metric. The practical lesson was that biological detail and model complexity do not automatically yield more stable out-of-sample prediction.

title: Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Breast Cancer
text:
Limitations
This was a time-bounded competition analysis rather than a peer-reviewed clinical prediction model. Sample size limited power to distinguish modest performance differences; fold-to-fold variability showed uncertainty; overall survival is a broad endpoint; and feature selection may be unstable in high-dimensional data. Independent external validation would be required before clinical use.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text: Peer-reviewed prospective cohort studynpj Vaccines · 2024

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Overview
This study evaluated the association between influenza vaccination and incident dementia and Parkinson’s disease among adults aged 60 years or older in the UK Biobank.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Research problem
Vaccination status, health factors, medications, and other covariates can change during follow-up. Treating repeatedly observed information as if it were fixed at baseline can obscure the timing of exposure and confounding.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Why it matters
A longitudinal design with time-updated information can better represent annual vaccination patterns and later neurodegenerative outcomes, while sensitivity analyses help make the limits of an observational association more transparent.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
My contribution
I contributed to the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data; manuscript drafting; and critical revision of the manuscript.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Data and study design
The analysis used linked UK Biobank primary-care, hospital, death-registry, and baseline data. It employed a prospective new-user design, defined influenza vaccination as a time-varying exposure measured in yearly intervals, and followed participants for incident dementia and Parkinson’s disease outcomes.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Statistical methods

Multivariable time-varying Cox regression
Adjustment for baseline and repeatedly measured covariates
Robust sandwich-type variance estimation for repeated measures
Secondary dose-response and subgroup analyses
Sensitivity analyses including marginal structural and competing-risk models

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Results and practical contribution
The publication reported an association between influenza vaccination and lower incident dementia risk, but not Parkinson’s disease incidence, after adjustment. Because this is observational evidence, the finding should not be interpreted as proving a causal preventive effect.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Limitations
The authors noted limitations in diagnostic accuracy for dementia subtypes and the possibility of residual or unmeasured confounding. Selection into the primary-care-linked cohort and exposure/outcome classification also affect generalizability.

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Outputs

 Peer-reviewed publication npj Vaccines · Open access

title: Influenza Vaccination and Neurodegenerative Disease Risk
text:
Reproducibility and availability
The article reports UK Biobank access procedures and links the study code through its code-availability statement. No participant-level data are redistributed here.

title: Longitudinal Proteomic and Extracellular-Vesicle Biomarker Analysis
text:
Overview
Within the DPPOS study at the GWU Biostatistics Center, I contribute to longitudinal proteomic analyses and extracellular-vesicle biomarker quality-control assessment related to cognitive aging in type 2 diabetes.

title: Longitudinal Proteomic and Extracellular-Vesicle Biomarker Analysis
text:
My contribution
I develop statistical analysis plans for longitudinal proteomic research and evaluate how extracellular-vesicle biomarker quality-control decisions affect downstream analyses.

title: Longitudinal Proteomic and Extracellular-Vesicle Biomarker Analysis
text:
Study context and data access
The work uses longitudinal data from the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study. DPPOS resources are available to qualified researchers by request through the NIDDK Central Repository. Project-specific biomarker data and results are not distributed through this site.

title: Longitudinal Proteomic and Extracellular-Vesicle Biomarker Analysis
text:
Current analytical focus
The ongoing work focuses on prespecifying analysis populations and timing, documenting biomarker quality-control decisions, planning longitudinal association analyses, and evaluating whether conclusions are sensitive to QC choices.
